Framework for Evaluating LSERO With Bilateral Contracting Using the Modeling Associated
with the ERCOT Reliability Standard

1. Purpose of This Framework

This document provides a concise outline of the analytical scope ERCOT should use to
evaluate LSERO with Bilateral Contracting, using the same modeling tools already proven
in prior ERCOT and PUCT studies. The goal is to determine:

• How much dispatchable generation is required for reliability

• How LSERO allocates that requirement fairly among LSEs

• How the resulting resource mix evolves

• How system‑wide operating costs change

• Whether LSERO lowers electricity costs for Texans

This is a technical framework, not an expansion of the prior filing.

2. Why the Current Market Must Be Studied

ERCOT’s energy‑only market is not producing new dispatchable plants and is not truly
competitive. Some LSEs effectively free‑ride on others’ dispatchable resources, and
scarcity pricing has failed to produce the investment needed for reliability.

Reliability is not optional. Texas must determine the most competitive and efficient way to
ensure adequate dispatchable capacity.

3. Core LSERO Structure to Be Evaluated

3.1 Determine the system‑wide dispatchable requirement

Using the ERCOT Reliability Standard, ERCOT identifies how much dispatchable capacity
is needed system‑wide to maintain reliability.

3.2 Allocate that requirement to each LSE

Each LSE’s LSERO obligation is based on its firm load, representing the non‑interruptible
demand that must be served under all system conditions. This ensures that reliability
responsibilities are aligned with the actual must‑serve demand each LSE imposes on the
ERCOT system.

If ERCOT determines that 50% of firm system load must be dispatchable, then each LSE
must ensure that 50% of its own firm load is backed by dispatchable resources.
 This eliminates free‑riding and creates a level competitive playing field.



3.3 Allow LSEs to meet the obligation through bilateral contracting

Each LSE may choose its own mix:

• Combined‑cycle plants

• Peaking plants

• Renewables

• Storage

• Long‑term bilateral contracts

• Self‑build or merchant procurement

This preserves competition and avoids central planning.

3.4 Allow retirements to occur naturally

As efficient CC plants enter, older steam units retire based on economics, improving
system heat rate and lowering operating costs.

4. Modeling Approach (Using the SERVOL Model)

ERCOT should evaluate LSERO using the SERVOL production‑cost model, the same tool
used by E3 in 2023. ERCOT already owns this model and can run it directly or through
consultants.

4.1 What the E3 study showed

The E3 analysis found that adding 13,000 MW of new dispatchable generation reduced
system‑wide annual operating costs by $5.9 billion.

This figure represents:

• The difference between total system operating cost with the new plants added

• And the cost without them

The annual savings can be used to lower electric rates.

4.2 SERVOL can be used with the ERCOT Reliability Standard to determine how much
dispatchable capacity is needed to meet the 0.1 reliability standard.
 At the E3 PCM workshop held Apr 17, 2023, the modeler confirmed that the SERVOL model
can be used in conjunction with the ERCOT Reliability Standard study to determine:

• How much dispatchable capacity is required to meet the reliability standard

• How that new capacity affects system‑wide operating costs

• How the resource mix evolves as new CC plants enter and older steam units retire

In short:

The LSERO with Bilateral Contracting framework simply ensures that once ERCOT
determines this requirement, each Load Serving Entity procures its proportional share
through bilateral contracting, consistent with its firm load obligation.

4.3 Why this matters for LSERO with Bilateral Contracting

LSERO is not theoretical. Bilateral contracting is widely used today!

It is a model‑verifiable market design that can be evaluated using tools ERCOT already
possesses.

5. Expected Outcomes to Be Evaluated

ERCOT’s study should determine whether LSERO:

• Improves reliability

• Eliminates free‑riding

• Restores true competition

• Encourages efficient CC plants

• Allows renewables and storage to compete fairly

• Reduces scarcity pricing

• Lowers system‑wide operating costs

• Lowers long‑term consumer rates

6. Conclusion

LSERO with Bilateral Contracting provides a competitive, transparent, and
model‑verifiable framework for ensuring reliability and lowering costs. ERCOT already has
the modeling tools needed to evaluate LSERO efficiently and thoroughly.
 

=== PUC LSERO Framework Letter.pdf ===
Chairman Thomas J. Gleeson and Commissioners

Public Utility Commission of Texas

1701 N. Congress Avenue

Austin, Texas 78701

Re: Project 58777 Framework for Evaluating LSERO with Bilateral Contracting is
attached -using the modeling associated with the ERCOT Reliability Standard scheduled
this year

Chairman Gleeson and Commissioners,

I am submitting the attached framework document to assist the commission with my
urgent request to have my revised market design submitted to ERCOT for analysis this year
along with the Reliability Standard study. They will both use the same model according to
testimony by L3 in a prior workshop. Both studies can proceed concurrently.

During the 2025 legislative hearings, ERCOT presented demand forecasts that underscore
the urgency of developing a market structure capable of supporting new dispatchable
generation. The Commission has adopted the ERCOT Reliability Standard, and ERCOT’s
modeling can determine the amount of dispatchable capacity required to meet that
standard. Given these conditions, I believe LSERO with Bilateral Contracting submitted in
my filing 58777offers a practical, competitive, and Texas‑appropriate path forward.

As outlined in my filings in Project No. 58777, LSERO with Bilateral Contracting is a simple
and familiar structure. It is a continuation of the bilateral contracting practices already
used extensively in ERCOT today. All LSEs have a reliability obligation. By ensuring that
every Load Serving Entity procures its proportional share of the dispatchable capacity
needed for reliability, LSERO guarantees a level playing field for enhanced wholesale
competition that doesn’t exist today.

Importantly, LSERO is model‑verifiable. At the April 17, 2023, PCM workshop, E3 staff
confirmed that the SERVOL modeling platform used in the E3 study is the same tool that
will be used to implement the ERCOT Reliability Standard. This means ERCOT already has
the analytical capability to determine how much dispatchable capacity is required and to
evaluate how LSERO allocates that requirement among LSEs. The attached framework
document outlines a concise, practical work scope for ERCOT’s study using tools already
in its possession. More dispatchable generation will be required; it is just a question of how
much will be needed. It will take more power plants, renewables, storage, and demand
side options to supply the massive demand growth.
 I am not asking the Commission to adopt LSERO with Bilateral Contracting; I am simply
requesting that the Commission refer this framework document outline to ERCOT for
technical evaluation. This is a modest, low‑risk step that allows ERCOT to analyze a
competitive, transparent, and reliability‑aligned market structure using existing models.
The results of that analysis — not this request — will determine whether LSERO with
Bilateral Contracting merits further consideration.

Thank you for your continued leadership in providing reliability through improved market
design. I am available to answer questions by phone or in writing at the Commission’s
request.

Respectfully submitted,

Thomas L. Darte

10503 Woodland Dr.

Greenville, Texas 75402

903‑454‑3424 (with voicemail)
